verified.name: js-draw (Eraser tool, PartialStroke mode)
verified.evidence: Source: https://github.com/personalizedrefrigerator/js-draw — packages/js-draw/src/tools/Eraser.ts defines `enum EraserMode { PartialStroke = 'partial-stroke', FullStroke = 'full-stroke' }`; in PartialStroke mode it calls `targetElem.withRegionErased(erasePath, viewport)` and re-adds the returned surviving segments (`toAdd.push(...targetElem.withRegionErased(...))`) — true geometric split, both halves survive as new components. FullStroke mode deletes whole elements; components lacking withRegionErased are whole-deleted in either mode. Verified by reading the raw file at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/personalizedrefrigerator/js-draw/main/packages/js-draw/src/tools/Eraser.ts
verified.eraserCodePointers: packages/js-draw/src/tools/Eraser.ts (mode switch + withRegionErased dispatch); the per-component split geometry lives in the components' withRegionErased implementations, notably packages/js-draw/src/components/Stroke.ts
verified.notes: STRONGEST candidate on both axes: the exact Drawboard/PKEraserTool semantic (vector split, halves survive), MIT TypeScript, public no-login demo (HTTP 200 verified 2026-07-20). It powers Joplin's freehand drawing. The demo's eraser UI exposes the partial/full mode toggle in its eraser panel — confirm which mode is default before benchmarking. Ideal for both the head-to-head harness and architecture theft.

verified.name: fabric.js EraserBrush (v5 core) / erase2d (v6+ successor)
verified.evidence: VISUALLY partial but NOT a geometric split — clip/mask accumulation. fabric 5.x source https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fabricjs/fabric.js/5.x/src/mixins/eraser_brush.mixin.js: 'While erasing the brush clips out the erasing path from canvas'; each object stores `this.eraser` (an Eraser group applied like a clipPath), SVG export via `mask="url(#...clipPathId)"` ('use <mask> to achieve erasing for svg'). v6+ moved this to @erase2d/fabric: its README documents `commit()` wrapping targets' clipPath in `new ClippingGroup([existingClipPath])` (https://github.com/ShaMan123/erase2d/blob/master/packages/fabric/README.md). Old demo http://fabricjs.com/erasing now 404s; live erase2d demo at https://shaman123.github.io/erase2d/ (HTTP 200 verified).
verified.repoUrl: https://github.com/ShaMan123/erase2d (v6 binding); https://github.com/fabricjs/fabric.js tree 5.x for the original
verified.eraserCodePointers: fabric 5.x: src/mixins/eraser_brush.mixin.js (EraserBrush + per-object `eraser` group + SVG mask export). erase2d: packages/core (eraser stroke build) and packages/fabric (ClippingGroup commit into target.clipPath)
verified.notes: Passes the user-visible test (touched part disappears, remainder survives) but the stroke remains ONE object with an ever-growing eraser mask — no split into two path objects, masks accumulate forever (perf + serialization weight), and PDF export would need mask flattening. Good benchmark rival for visual semantics; architecturally it is the design your KAL-366 work deliberately avoided (capsule split beats mask accumulation for PDF-native output).

verified.name: Paper.js (no built-in eraser; DIY boolean-subtract eraser)
verified.evidence: Paper.js ships NO eraser tool, but its boolean engine does true splitting. Reference implementation: 'Paper.js Vector Erase' gist https://gist.github.com/beardicus/8cbe9511d43e3fb58d76e336f76f4eb2 — live phase fakes erase with a 'source-out' blend group; on mouseup the eraser path is outlined (offset.js), then `var result = item.subtract(deleteShape, {trace: false, insert: false})` — 'each item that overlaps with the deletion shape is subtracted from, and if the result contains multiple pieces, they're preserved' (surviving pieces re-inserted via insertChildren). `trace:false` makes subtract operate on the stroke as an open path, i.e. genuine split-with-survivors. API docs: paperjs.org/reference/pathitem/#subtract and #divide.
verified.playgroundUrl: http://sketch.paperjs.org/ (paste the gist code to get a drivable eraser)
verified.eraserCodePointers: src/path/PathItem.Boolean.js in paper.js (subtract/divide, the trace option); the gist itself for the eraser-capsule outlining + subtract + multi-piece reinsertion pattern
verified.notes: 'likely-partial' only because the split lives in a community gist, not the library — the boolean engine itself is mature and confirmed to preserve pieces. Best architecture-theft target for the MATH (open-path boolean subtract ≈ your capsule engine); as a benchmark rival you must first assemble the demo (5-minute paste into sketch.paperjs.org).

verified.name: Miro (pen + Precision Eraser)
verified.evidence: Miro shipped a dedicated 'Precision eraser' (announced ~Dec 2020) explicitly to fix the old whole-delete complaint: community idea 'Erase only a piece of line' delivered — https://community.miro.com/ideas/erase-only-a-piece-of-line-3134; Help Center Pen article documents two erasers on the toolbar, the precision one erasing 'part of a drawing' by click-hold-drag over it while the rest of the pen line survives — https://help.miro.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017730573-Pen (help page 403s to plain fetch; content confirmed via search index + community thread https://community.miro.com/ask-the-community-45/how-can-i-erase-only-a-certain-part-of-a-figure-3989).
verified.notes: Strongest closed-source browser reference for the Drawboard semantic: two-eraser model (whole-stroke eraser + precision/partial eraser) matches your product design exactly. Free account is enough; canvas is WebGL/canvas-rendered so verification in harness should count surviving stroke objects via undo/redo or export, not DOM. Internals (true split into two stroke objects vs outline boolean) unverified — closed source; classify the observable behavior in your harness.
verified.skepticReason: Refutation attempt failed — primary sources support partial-erase. (1) Official Miro Help Center "Pen" article (https://help.miro.com/hc/en-us/articles/360017730573-Pen — 403s to plain fetch; read via live browser session) documents TWO distinct erasers and itself draws the whole-vs-partial line: the classic Eraser ("swipe across the drawings... the eraser removes pen drawings only") deletes whole strokes, while "If you need to erase part of a drawing, you can use the Precision eraser tool. Just select the tool, then click and hold while going over the part of the drawing you want to erase." So the evidence was NOT a different-eraser confusion — the docs explicitly contrast the two. (2) Not desktop-only: the same article lists "Available on: browser version, Desktop app, Tablet app" with no platform restriction on the precision eraser. (3) Not raster: Miro pen drawings are vector board objects (selectable via Select/Lasso, deletable via Delete key per the same article), and the Miro Community Team's delivery note says the Precision Eraser "lets you erase just part of a pen line without removing the whole drawing" — surviving remainder semantics, no bitmap/pixel-mask language anywhere (https://community.miro.com/ideas/erase-only-a-piece-of-line-3134, corroborated at https://community.miro.com/ask-the-community-45/how-can-i-erase-only-a-certain-part-of-a-figure-3989). (4) Not an old version: article updated ~7 months ago; feature is current. TWO CAVEATS for the caller: (a) the original claim's date is WRONG — the community idea was marked Delivered on 2025-12-04, so this is a LATE-2025 feature, not "~Dec 2020" (the 2020 date is roughly when the idea was requested); (b) docs state partial-erase behavior but do not literally describe the internal representation (true vector split vs masking), and live verification is impossible without a Miro account (no public no-login playground — also a demerit for the Playwright race harness). Behaviorally, confirmed-partial stands.

verified.name: Microsoft Whiteboard (web / Teams meeting whiteboard)
verified.evidence: Teams meeting whiteboard eraser has a double-click options menu with 'Erase entire stroke' as an explicit MODE — implying the other/default mode is partial: https://www.iorad.com/player/2130088/Microsoft-Teams---How-to-set-eraser-to-erase-entire-strokes-in-your-meeting-whiteboard. Microsoft update notes describe a velocity-adaptive 'partial eraser': 'the faster you erase the bigger it gets... the same eraser offers the precision you would need' (Whiteboard What's-new/App Store release notes, see https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoft_365blog/whats-new-for-microsoft-whiteboard---november-2022/3669360 and https://apps.apple.com/us/app/microsoft-whiteboard/id1352499399). History caveat: the 2021 Fluid redesign temporarily REPLACED partial erase with whole-stroke erase (https://futurework.blog/2021/10/27/new-whiteboard/), and the current support doc lists only a single Eraser tool with no mode detail (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/draw-and-ink-in-whiteboard-43bd83c0-4a0f-498b-824c-3c5bb480d787).
verified.notes: This is the same company/ink stack as the GetEraseResult semantic you're targeting, so if partial mode is live in the web build it is the canonical reference. But feature churn (removed 2021, re-added later, platform-dependent) means you must verify in the web app with a Microsoft account before spending benchmark time. Marked likely-partial, not confirmed, for the WEB build specifically.
verified.skepticReason: Refutation failed; evidence corroborates likely-partial. Timeline from primary observers: old Whiteboard had partial erase; the Oct 2021 Fluid redesign temporarily regressed to whole-stroke-only (futurework.blog 2021-10-27: "Erase portion of the ink has been replaced with eraser that removes the entire ink stroke"); Aug 2022 the regression was reversed — futurework.blog 2022-08-19 quotes: "Eraser is now defaulting removing a partial stroke, just like in the Whiteboard before this new fluid version," with a click-again eraser menu to switch behavior; Nov 2022 Microsoft's own techcommunity blog announced the velocity-adaptive partial eraser rolling out to M365 commercial. Skeptic checks all cleared: (a) not a different mode — "Erase entire stroke" in the iorad Teams tutorial is the explicit ALTERNATE menu mode, confirming partial is default; (b) not desktop-only — post-2021 Whiteboard is one Fluid/web codebase and both the Aug 2022 observation and the iorad tutorial are of the Teams/web client; (c) not raster — ink is vector Fluid objects and an object-aware "erase entire stroke" mode is incoherent for a bitmap eraser; (d) not an old version — whole-stroke was the temporary 2021–22 state, partial is both original and restored-current default. Caveats keeping this at confirmed-classification rather than screen-verified: whiteboard.office.com requires M365 login (no public no-login playground — poor candidate for the Playwright race harness regardless), current support doc is mode-silent, no post-2022 primary source re-affirms, and split-into-two-surviving-halves was inferred from the vector model + Microsoft wording, not observed frame-by-frame. Classification "likely-partial" stands.

verified.name: OneNote for the web (Draw tab point erasers)
verified.evidence: OneNote's documented eraser model: 'Eraser (small, medium, and large): Drag with this eraser over a line to erase part of a line. Stroke eraser: Click a line to erase an entire line' — and partial erase explicitly creates new shapes ('by erasing part of an oval, you can create an arc'), i.e. true stroke splitting: https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/microsoft-r-onenote-r-2010/9780735664784/ch11s04.html and https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/onenote/onenote-help-and-learning/learn-more-about-drawing-tools ('point eraser which has multiple thickness options... more precise when erasing a small section of the ink'). The web-specific support article only says 'Click Draw > Eraser, and then erase the notes' with no size/mode detail: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/write-notes-and-draw-in-onenote-for-the-web-88ac049d-08a9-427b-a363-1266f606b89b.
verified.notes: The desktop point eraser is the textbook GetEraseResult splitter. Whether the WEB canvas implements the same point-eraser split (vs whole-stroke only) is NOT confirmed by any doc I found — the web Draw tab has historically lagged desktop. One 5-minute logged-in check (draw line, drag small eraser through middle, see if two halves survive and select independently) settles it. Needs a Microsoft account; the ribbon UI is standard DOM so Playwright can drive tool selection, ink canvas is pointer-event driven.

verified.name: Canva Whiteboard / Canva Draw
verified.evidence: Canva Draw help + third-party walkthroughs: after drawing, an Eraser with adjustable brush size lets you 'brush over the areas you want to erase' i.e. erase parts of a drawing, and a newer option adds a transparency/opacity mode that reduces stroke opacity instead of removing it: https://www.canva.com/help/draw-in-canva/ (403s to plain fetch; corroborated by https://weignitegrowth.com/how-to-erase-in-canva-eraser-tool/ and https://www.bwillcreative.com/how-to-erase-in-canva/).
verified.notes: Partial in EFFECT, but the opacity-mode option is a hint the implementation may be mask/brush-based rather than a true vector split with surviving halves — could be closer to pixel-raster-only semantics on a vector container. Needs a Canva account and their editor is heavily canvas-rendered. Low priority: verify split vs mask only if you run out of better references.

verified.name: Limnu
verified.evidence: Limnu FAQ (fetched 2026-07-20, https://limnu.com/faq-support/): 'You can use the erase tool — this is great for taking out just a part of your drawing.' Their diagram blog recommends drawing a full line then using erase for dashed-line 'dropouts' — only meaningful if erase punches gaps mid-stroke: https://limnu.com/anatomy-of-a-whiteboard-diagram/.
verified.notes: Partial in effect, but Limnu's whole pitch is texture-realistic marker rendering on canvas, so the erase may be raster-style (paint-over/gap in the rendered texture) rather than a vector split producing two surviving stroke objects — strokes ARE selectable/movable objects per their FAQ, which muddies it. Closed source, small product, signup required (free trial gated by card after trial per FAQ). Low priority for the harness; only worth it as a rendering-quality reference.

verified.name: Xournal++ (default 'Standard' eraser)
verified.eraserCodePointers: src/core/control/tools/EraseHandler.cpp (erase()/eraseStroke(), ~L47-130: dispatches ERASER_TYPE_DELETE_STROKE=whole vs default=partial); src/core/model/Stroke.cpp L583+ intersectWithPaddedBox() (computes entry/exit path parameters of the eraser box against the stroke centerline); src/core/model/eraser/ErasableStroke.{h,cpp} (remainingSections is a UnionOfIntervals<PathParameter>; getStrokes() at ErasableStroke.cpp L232 clones each surviving interval into a NEW Stroke via stroke.cloneSection(), with closed-stroke first/last merge via cloneCircularSectionOfClosedStroke); src/core/model/eraser/ErasableStrokeOverlapTree.cpp (self-overlap rendering); src/core/model/eraser/PaddedBox.h; src/core/undo/EraseUndoAction.cpp
verified.evidence: Verified by reading source at master HEAD (cloned 2026-07-20). EraseHandler.cpp: comment 'Handle eraser event: "Delete Stroke" and "Standard"'; default branch builds PaddedBox{{x,y}, halfEraserSize, halfEraserSize + paddingCoeff*s->getWidth()} — i.e. WIDTH-AWARE: the eraser box is padded by a cap-style coefficient times the stroke's own width (PADDING_COEFFICIENT_CAP), so fat strokes are hit at their rim, not just centerline. ToolEnums.h L157: ERASER_TYPE_DEFAULT / WHITEOUT / DELETE_STROKE. Files: https://github.com/xournalpp/xournalpp/blob/master/src/core/control/tools/EraseHandler.cpp , https://github.com/xournalpp/xournalpp/blob/master/src/core/model/eraser/ErasableStroke.cpp
verified.notes: BEST architecture-theft target for the Drawboard/PKEraserTool semantic. Technique = parametric interval cutting on the centerline: intersection yields (segment index, t) PathParameters, erased spans are removed from a UnionOfIntervals, survivors become independent strokes preserving stroke style/width (never converted to filled outline). Also maintains a live 'erasure in progress' render (ErasableStrokeView) before commit — same live/commit split as our KAL-366 design. Eraser modes: Standard = partial split (default), Whiteout = paints white stroke, Delete Stroke = whole-only. C++/GTK desktop app, no browser build — code-reading target only.

verified.name: Rnote ('Split colliding strokes' eraser mode)
verified.eraserCodePointers: crates/rnote-engine/src/store/trash_comp.rs L129+ split_colliding_strokes() (the splitter); crates/rnote-engine/src/pens/eraser.rs L228-243 (mode dispatch: TrashCollidingStrokes -> store.trash_colliding_strokes, SplitCollidingStrokes -> store.split_colliding_strokes); crates/rnote-engine/src/pens/pensconfig/eraserconfig.rs (enum EraserStyle { TrashCollidingStrokes, SplitCollidingStrokes }, default = Trash, eraser_bounds() = AABB of width 12.0 default); crates/rnote-compose/src/penpath/mod.rs L149 PenPath::hittest()
verified.evidence: Verified by reading source at main HEAD (cloned 2026-07-20). trash_comp.rs doc comment: 'Remove colliding stroke segments with the given bounds. The stroke is then split.' Implementation: PenPath::hittest(&eraser_bounds, stroke_width*0.5) returns hit SEGMENT INDICES (per-segment hitboxes loosened by half the stroke width — width-aware); the segment list is sliced between consecutive hits; each surviving slice with >1 segment becomes a new BrushStroke::from_penpath with the same style; the original keeps the pre-first-hit prefix or is trashed if empty. Files: https://github.com/flxzt/rnote/blob/main/crates/rnote-engine/src/store/trash_comp.rs , https://github.com/flxzt/rnote/blob/main/crates/rnote-engine/src/pens/pensconfig/eraserconfig.rs
verified.notes: Second-best code-reading target; Rust, very readable. Technique = segment-granularity interval cutting (removes whole hit segments, not sub-segment t-splits like Xournal++ — slightly coarser cuts, and it drops sliver splits with <2 segments, i.e. built-in sliver cull like ours). IMPORTANT: default eraser mode is TrashCollidingStrokes (whole-delete); the partial behavior is the second toggle in the eraser sidebar (eraserpage.ui). GTK4 desktop only, no web build.

verified.name: Inkscape eraser tool (CUT mode)
verified.eraserCodePointers: src/ui/tools/eraser-tool.cpp — modes DELETE/CUT/CLIP (~L94-105); _booleanErase() (~L556-594): non-zero-width eraser stroke is unioned (pathUnion) then boolean-differenced against targets via operands.pathDiff(true,true); zero-width uses operands.pathCut(true,true) (path cutting/splitting); break-apart branch (~L589) operands.breakApart(...) makes each surviving fragment a separate object. Underlying boolean ops live in src/path/path-boolop.cpp (livarot).
verified.evidence: Fetched and analyzed https://gitlab.com/inkscape/inkscape/-/raw/master/src/ui/tools/eraser-tool.cpp on 2026-07-20: three modes; CUT applies boolean difference of the eraser's calligraphic stroke shape against touched items; with 'break apart' pref on, breakApart() yields separate surviving pieces. Docs: https://inkscape.gitlab.io/inkscape/doxygen/eraser-tool_8cpp.html and Inkscape 1.x eraser toolbar reference (delete/cut/clip + break-apart toggle).
verified.notes: Partial, but via BOOLEAN OPS ON OUTLINE GEOMETRY — the exact 'converts stroked ink to filled outline' failure family our KAL-366 root fix banned: cutting a stroked open path generally yields filled outline fragments, not centerline sub-strokes with live stroke style. Valuable as the contrast/anti-pattern reference and for robust boolean-op code (livarot), not as the semantic target. Desktop app (GTK); no drivable browser build (inkscape.org web demos are not the eraser).

verified.name: OpenBoard eraser
verified.eraserCodePointers: src/domain/UBGraphicsScene.cpp L1034 eraseLineTo(): eraser drag segment -> UBGeometryUtils::lineToPolygon(line, width) -> QPainterPath; for each intersecting UBGraphicsPolygonItem: fully-contained items removed whole, else itemPainterPath.subtracted(eraserPath.toReversed()) with Qt::WindingFill, then newPath.simplified().toFillPolygons() and each fill polygon becomes a NEW UBGraphicsPolygonItem replacing the original (mAddedItems/mRemovedItems for undo).
verified.evidence: Verified by reading source at master HEAD (cloned 2026-07-20). Source comment: 'remove full polygon item and replace it by a couple of polygons which create the same stroke without the part that intersects with the eraser'. https://github.com/OpenBoard-org/OpenBoard/blob/master/src/domain/UBGraphicsScene.cpp (eraseLineTo)
verified.notes: Partial and the halves survive, but strokes in OpenBoard are ALREADY stored as filled variable-width polygons (one polygon item per pen segment group), so the eraser is pure QPainterPath boolean subtraction on filled geometry — no centerline model exists to preserve. Interesting for: capsule-shaped eraser swept-segment polygon (lineToPolygon), reversed-path winding trick for hole punching, and add/remove undo bookkeeping. Qt desktop app, not browser-drivable.

verified.name: WPF System.Windows.Ink point eraser (InkCanvas EraseByPoint / Stroke.GetEraseResult) — the canonical Microsoft partial-erase implementation, fully open source
verified.eraserCodePointers: All under src/Microsoft.DotNet.Wpf/src/ in dotnet/wpf (paths verified via GitHub API 2026-07-20): PresentationCore/System/Windows/Ink/Stroke.cs + Stroke2.cs (public GetEraseResult/Erase), StrokeCollection.cs/StrokeCollection2.cs (StrokeCollection.Erase replace-in-place), IncrementalHitTester.cs (IncrementalStrokeHitTester — live per-move point-erase engine, fires StrokeHit with GetPointEraseResults()); PresentationCore/MS/internal/Ink/ErasingStroke.cs (the swept eraser-shape path), StrokeNode.cs, StrokeNodeOperations.cs + StrokeNodeOperations2.cs (62KB+23KB of exact contour-vs-contour hit math), EllipticalNodeOperations.cs, StrokeIntersection.cs, StrokeFIndices.cs (parametric fractional-index cut points), StylusShape.cs, Lasso.cs; PresentationFramework/MS/Internal/Ink/EraserBehavior.cs (InkCanvas EraseByPoint editing-mode wiring, 18KB).
verified.evidence: Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.ink.stroke.geteraseresult — 'returns the segments of the current Stroke that are outside the specified bounds'; StrokeCollection.Erase docs: 'If the specified area is through the middle of a Stroke, the erase removes that Stroke and creates two new strokes'; GetEraseResult is pure (original Stroke unchanged). How-to with StylusShape eraser tip: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/advanced/how-to-erase-ink-on-a-custom-control. Source files listed in eraserCodePointers verified to exist in dotnet/wpf main.
verified.notes: ARCHITECTURE TO STEAL (this is the reference semantic): (1) eraser = StylusShape (ellipse/rect) swept along the pointer path — ErasingStroke builds an incremental capsule/Minkowski sweep per pointer-move; (2) hit test is contour-vs-contour: the ink stroke's own per-point pressure-scaled node shapes (StrokeNode/EllipticalNodeOperations), NOT centerline — rim contact cuts; (3) cuts are parametric StrokeFIndices along the stroke spine; surviving segments become NEW Stroke objects with endpoints interpolated exactly at the cut boundary, inheriting DrawingAttributes and interpolated pressure/width at the cut; (4) pure-function GetEraseResult + mutating StrokeCollection.Erase split lets live preview and commit share one engine; (5) cut ends render with the normal StylusTip geometry (ellipse tip = rounded caps at cut ends). Windows-only WPF app so not raceable in a Chromium harness, but a small WPF InkCanvas EditingMode=EraseByPoint app is the ground-truth oracle for split correctness. Mirrors our own d07b6e2f/65f37906 capsule-engine approach — good for validating our math 1:1.

verified.name: Apple PencilKit PKEraserTool (.bitmap type = partial on vector strokes via maskedPathRanges; .vector type = whole-stroke)
verified.evidence: Apple docs (via developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/documentation/pencilkit/pkerasertool.json): 'The eraser tool's type determines whether the canvas removes entire items or just the portion of an item that it touches' — .vector removes whole strokes, .bitmap removes touched portions; init(_:width:) + width property exist for fixed-width erasers (width control shipped in the iOS 16.4 SDK era; base tool iOS 13+). Crucially the 'bitmap' name is misleading: strokes REMAIN vector — WWDC20 'Inspect, modify, and construct PencilKit drawings' (https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2020/10148/) documents PKStroke.maskedPathRanges: an array of parametric ranges of the B-spline path surviving after erase; a stroke with holes has multiple ranges, and can have zero ranges. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/pencilkit/pkerasertool
verified.notes: The SECOND canonical architecture, alternative to WPF's split-into-new-strokes: keep ONE stroke object + a list of surviving parametric ranges (mask), render only masked ranges. Pros: original point/pressure data untouched, trivial undo, holes natural. Cons: hit-testing and export must consume ranges. PencilKit path is a uniform cubic B-spline of points carrying size/force, so cutting in parameter space preserves variable width exactly — same principle as WPF's StrokeFIndices. Drivable only via iOS Simulator (ios-simulator-skill exists locally) — not raceable in the Chromium harness, but a Freeform/Notes side-by-side video is legit evidence footage. WATCH OUT classifying competitors: many apps copy the PencilKit naming, so 'vector eraser' in an iOS app's UI often means WHOLE-stroke delete and 'pixel eraser' means partial — the names invert intuition.
